title: Does the Opening Range Breakout + VWAP Strategy Work? | What Doesn't Work
snippet:
An 84-trade intraday sweep found a tiny gross edge that costs erased, while the VWAP filter changed none of the opening-range trades.

 Published 8/15/2026
...
Mark the high and low of the first 15 regular-session minutes. Buy the first one-minute close above that range when price is above a rising session VWAP, or short the mirror image below a falling VWAP. Put the standard stop at the far side of the range and target another 1.5 opening-range widths beyond the breakout.

I tested that rule on Nasdaq and S&P 500 index CFDs, then used five liquid US stocks as a broader check. Across 84 trades, the pooled result was +1.26 basis points per trade before costs and -0.86 bps after modest round-trip costs. Three of seven markets finished positive under the risk-sizing model.

The surprising part was the filter: removing VWAP changed zero trades. In this sample, a one-minute close beyond the full 15-minute range was already on the expected side of VWAP with the expected slope.

The verdict is inconclusive, with low confidence. A near-flat result over five index sessions and 15 stock sessions is useful ... enough evidence to approve or bury an intraday idea.
...
The opening range is the high and low printed from 9:30 to 9:45 a.m. Eastern time. The idea is that heavy activity near the open reveals institutional intent. Once the range is fixed, wait rather than guessing inside it.
